A **symplectic vector space** is a pair $(V,\omega)$ consisting of a
finite-dimensional real vector space $V$ and an alternating bilinear form
$\omega:V\times V\to\mathbb R$ for which

$$\omega^\flat:V\longrightarrow V^*,\qquad \omega^\flat(v)=\omega(v,\,·),$$

is an isomorphism. Equivalently, $\omega(v,w)=0$ for every $w\in V$ implies
$v=0$. The equivalence also follows from the radical clause in
[[thm-alternating-forms-have-a-symplectic-normal-form]]. The zero vector space,
with its unique alternating form, is included: its map to its dual is the
unique isomorphism.

Every symplectic vector space $(V,\omega)$ has dimension $2n$ for a unique
$n\ge 0$. It has a basis $e_1,\ldots,e_n,f_1,\ldots,f_n$ in which
$\omega(e_i,f_j)=\delta_{ij}$ and all $e$--$e$ and $f$--$f$ pairings vanish.

Every continuous group homomorphism $\varphi:\mathbb R\to\mathbb T$ from the
additive line to the multiplicative unit circle
([[lem-unit-circle-is-a-compact-metrizable-topological-group]]) is
$\varphi(t)=\exp(2\pi i\xi t)$ for a unique $\xi\in\mathbb R$; conversely every
such map $\varphi_{\xi}(t)=\exp(2\pi i\xi t)$ is a continuous character of the
additive line.

(1) For locally compact Hausdorff abelian groups $G_{1},\dots,G_{n}$ the map
$$\Phi:\widehat{G_{1}}\times\cdots\times\widehat{G_{n}}\to\widehat{G_{1}\times\cdots\times G_{n}},\qquad \Phi(\gamma_{1},\dots,\gamma_{n})\big((x_{1},\dots,x_{n})\big):=\prod_{j}\gamma_{j}(x_{j}),$$
is an isomorphism of topological groups for the product topologies (choice-free,
finite $n$). (2) If $(G_{i})_{i\in I}$ is a family of discrete abelian groups and
$G=\bigoplus_{i}G_{i}$ is their algebraic direct sum equipped with the discrete
topology ([[def-direct-sum-of-a-family-of-modules]]), then, assuming the Axiom
of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]), $\widehat G$ is topologically isomorphic to
the product $\prod_{i}\widehat{G_{i}}$ with the product topology. No claim is
made here about a direct sum carrying the subspace topology of the product of
non-discrete factors.

Let $N$ and $H$ be groups ([[def-group]]), and let $\alpha:H\to\operatorname{Aut}(N)$ be an action by automorphisms ([[def-action-by-automorphisms]]). The **external semidirect product** $N\rtimes_\alpha H$ is the set $N\times H$ with multiplication

$$(n,h)(n',h')=\bigl(n\alpha_h(n'),hh'\bigr).$$

When the action is clear, the subscript is omitted.

An **action of a group $H$ on a group $N$ by automorphisms** is a homomorphism

$$\alpha:H\longrightarrow\operatorname{Aut}(N).$$

Here automorphisms are those of [[def-group-isomorphism-and-automorphism]]. Writing $\alpha_h=\alpha(h)$, this means that every $\alpha_h$ is an automorphism of $N$, $\alpha_{hk}=\alpha_h\circ\alpha_k$, and $\alpha_1=\operatorname{id}_N$. Equivalently, by [[thm-group-actions-correspond-to-homomorphisms]], it is a group action ([[def-group-action]]) on the underlying set of $N$ for which every acting permutation is an automorphism.

derivations.claim: In coordinates from [F2], bilinearity gives $\omega((q,p),(q',p'))=q\cdot p'-p\cdot q'$. For three vectors $v,w,u$,$\omega(v,w)+\omega(v+w,u)=\omega(v,w)+\omega(v,u)+\omega(w,u) =\omega(w,u)+\omega(v,w+u).$Thus $c(v,w)=-\frac12\omega(v,w)$ satisfies the normalized 2-cocycle identity $c(v,w)+c(v+w,u)=c(w,u)+c(v,w+u)$. Substitution in the group law proves associativity; $\omega(v,0)=\omega(0,v)=0$ gives identity $(0,0)$, and $\omega(v,-v)=0$ gives inverse $(-v,-t)$. Addition and $\omega$ are continuous, so multiplication and inverse are continuous. The underlying finite-dimensional Euclidean space $V\times\mathbb R$ is locally compact and second countable.

An element $(v,t)$ commutes with every $(w,0)$ exactly when $\omega(v,w)=0$ for all $w$. Nondegeneracy in [F1] forces $v=0$, and each $(0,t)$ is central by the product formula. Hence the center is the displayed central coordinate. The projection $(v,t)\mapsto v$ is onto with kernel $\{(0,t):t\in\mathbb R\}$, proving exactness of the central extension in the definition.

For $q\in K$ and $(p,t)\in N$, direct multiplication gives $(q,0,0)(0,p,t)(-q,0,0)=(0,p,t-q\cdot p)$; thus $\alpha_q(p,t)=(p,t-q\cdot p)$. This is an automorphism because it is additive, has inverse $\alpha_{-q}$, and $\alpha_{q+q'}=\alpha_q\alpha_{q'}$. Every group element has the unique factorization$(q,p,z)=(0,p,z-q\cdot p/2)(q,0,0).$Therefore $(n,q)\mapsto n(q,0,0)$ is a bijection from the semidirect product of [F4] to $H(V,\omega)$; the conjugation computation makes it a homomorphism. Its coordinate formula and inverse are continuous, so it is a topological group isomorphism.

Apply [F3] to $N\cong\mathbb R^{n+1}$. Rescaling the coordinates by $2\pi$ gives every character exactly once as $\chi_{a,\mu}(p,t)=e^{i(a\cdot p+\mu t)}$. Since $\alpha_{-q}(p,t)=(p,t+q\cdot p)$, composition yields$q\cdot\chi_{a,\mu}=\chi_{a+\mu q,\mu}.$

When $\mu=\lambda\ne0$, the map $q\mapsto a+\lambda q$ is a bijection of $\mathbb R^n$ with itself. It is continuous with continuous inverse $a\mapsto(a-a_0)/\lambda$, so the orbit through $(a_0,\lambda)$ is all of $\widehat N_\lambda$ and its stabilizer is $\{0\}$. This proves the free transitive orbit and stabilizer claims.
Steps 1.1–4.1 establish the group, topological, central, semidirect, and dual-orbit assertions, including the zero-dimensional case $n=0$ where the Lagrangian subgroup $K$ is trivial.

boundaries.evidence: At n=0 the Lagrangian K is trivial, N=R, and H=R; 5.1 explicitly includes this empty-coordinate case.
Step 3.1 gives the dual-action formula, which fixes every character with central coordinate zero.
For one mode n=1, alpha_q(p,t)=(p,t-qp) and the nonzero-lambda orbit is the affine line a+lambda q, with trivial stabilizer (2.2–4.1).

boundaries.reason: Nondegeneracy of omega is essential in 2.1 to force a central v to be zero; degenerate forms are excluded. Lambda=0 is excluded only from the free/transitive orbit assertion.
The Euclidean group and character formulas use all real coordinates, with no endpoint restriction.

boundaries.evidence: Local source sections: Statement; Proof. A symplectic basis is a single finite-dimensional selection. The identity character and (0,0,0) explicitly witness the required nonempty sets; no indexed family of choices is used.
Commuting with every (w,0) forces omega(v,w)=0 for all w by the product comparison in 2.1; nondegeneracy then forces v=0.
If v=0 then the cocycle with every w is zero, so (0,t) commutes with the group. Step 2.1 proves the reverse direction of its centrality criterion.

finite_checks.claim: The central cocycle satisfies the associativity identity.
The semidirect coordinate factorization is exact.

Exact real-character and finite-product-dual suppliers give chi_(a,mu); dual action is a->a+mu q, free transitive only for mu!=0, including n=0. Uses only finite-product choice-free clause. Let $\mathbb N=\{1,2,\ldots\}$ be the countable mode set. For each $n$ take the universal finite-mode C*-algebra $\mathsf{CAR}_n$ whose dense algebraic presentation is [[def-finite-mode-car-algebra]]. Identify each stage with its image in the next under the isometric inclusion of [[lem-finite-mode-car-canonical-inclusions-are-isometric]]. The inclusions are compatible, injective, and preserve the C*-norm. Their union $\mathsf{CAR}_{\mathrm{loc}}=\bigcup_{n\ge0}\mathsf{CAR}_n$ is therefore a normed $*$-algebra with norm $\|x\|=\|x\|_{\mathsf{CAR}_n}$ whenever $x\in\mathsf{CAR}_n$; isometry makes this independent of the stage. Define the **countably infinite-mode CAR C*-algebra** $\mathsf{CAR}_{\mathbb N}$ to be the norm completion of $\mathsf{CAR}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ in the sense of [[def-c-star-algebra]]. Its canonical generator $a_j$ is the image of the $j$th finite-mode generator in any stage $n\ge j$. The C*-axioms pass to the completion because each finite stage satisfies them and multiplication and involution are continuous. The universal property of this inductive-limit construction is proved in [[thm-countable-mode-car-has-universal-inductive-limit-norm]].

The existence of this particular completion needs no choice principle. Let $\pi_n:\mathsf{CAR}_n\to M_{2^n}(\mathbb C)$ be the occupation-basis isomorphism of [[thm-finite-mode-car-algebra-is-full-matrix-algebra]], and let $D_n\subseteq\mathsf{CAR}_n$ be the inverse image of $M_{2^n}(\mathbb Q(i))$, where $\mathbb Q(i)=\{a+ib:a,b\in\mathbb Q\}$. Write $\mathbb N_0=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}$ for coding indices, to distinguish it from the positive mode set $\mathbb N$. The theorem [[thm-rationals-countable]] supplies a surjection $\mathbb N_0\to\mathbb Q$, and pairing two such indices by [[thm-n-cross-n-countable]] gives an explicit enumeration of $\mathbb Q(i)$. In these coordinates the canonical inclusion is $A\mapsto A\otimes I_2$ ([[lem-finite-mode-car-canonical-inclusions-are-isometric]]), so $D_n\subseteq D_{n+1}$. Each finite array of Gaussian rationals is coded by a finite tuple in $\mathbb N_0$; repeated pairing, followed by pairing with the stage index, enumerates $D=\bigcup_{n\ge0}D_n$ without choosing from a family of stage enumerations. Entrywise approximation of real and imaginary parts by rationals ([[lem-rat-embeds-dense]]) shows Gaussian-rational matrices are dense in each finite-dimensional matrix stage: in fixed size $m$, $\|A-B\|_{\mathrm{op}}\le m\max_{r,s}|a_{rs}-b_{rs}|$. Hence $D$ is dense in $\mathsf{CAR}_{\mathrm{loc}}$.

Concretely, form the set of Cauchy sequences in $\mathsf{CAR}_{\mathrm{loc}}$, identify two sequences when the norm of their termwise difference tends to zero, and use the limiting norm and termwise algebra operations. Write $\widehat d([a_n],[b_n])=\lim_n\|a_n-b_n\|$ for the resulting completion metric. Products are well defined because Cauchy sequences are bounded and $\|x_my_m-x_ny_n\|\le\|x_m\|\,\|y_m-y_n\|+\|x_m-x_n\|\,\|y_n\|$; the involution is isometric. Thus the completion is a normed $*$-algebra, and its C*-identity passes to limits. It is complete without Countable Choice: the constant-sequence image of $\mathsf{CAR}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is dense in the sequence-class completion, so $D$ is dense there too. Fix the explicit enumeration $q:\mathbb N_0\twoheadrightarrow D$. For any Cauchy sequence $(x_m)$ of completion points, let $d_m$ be the first $q(r)$ within $2^{-m}$ of $x_m$. The least-index rule defines each $d_m$ uniquely. The triangle inequality shows $(d_m)$ is Cauchy; for $m,n$ sufficiently large, $\widehat d(x_m,d_n)\le\widehat d(x_m,x_n)+2^{-n}$ is arbitrarily small, so the class $[d_n]$ is the limit of $(x_m)$. Hence this sequence-class construction is a completion of $\mathsf{CAR}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and defines $\mathsf{CAR}_{\mathbb N}$ choice-free. Its canonical generators and inductive-limit norm are unchanged.

For $n\ge0$, let $\iota_n:\mathsf{CAR}_n\to\mathsf{CAR}_{n+1}$ be the unique unital $*$-homomorphism sending each of the first $n$ annihilation and creation generators to the generator with the same index. Here $\mathsf{CAR}_n$ is the universal finite-mode C*-algebra of [[thm-finite-mode-car-algebra-is-full-matrix-algebra]]. Then $\iota_n$ is isometric and injective. Under the occupation-basis identifications $\mathcal F_{n+1}\cong\mathcal F_n\otimes\mathbb C^2$, it is represented by $A\mapsto A\otimes I_2$.

For every integer $n\ge0$, the universal finite-mode CAR $*$-algebra $\mathsf{CAR}^{\mathrm{alg}}_n$ of [[def-finite-mode-car-algebra]] is $*$-isomorphic to $\operatorname{End}(\mathcal F_n)\cong M_{2^n}(\mathbb C)$ under the occupation representation of [[lem-finite-mode-car-occupation-matrix-units]], where $\operatorname{End}(\mathcal F_n)$ denotes all complex-linear endomorphisms under composition. Give this matrix algebra the operator norm and conjugate-transpose involution; it is a C*-algebra in the sense of [[def-c-star-algebra]]. Every unital $*$-representation on a nonzero Hilbert space is unitarily identified with the matrix action on the occupation coordinate tensored with the identity on one Hilbert space, and is therefore isometric. Consequently the universal C*-norm, the supremum of operator norms over these representations, equals the matrix norm, so the universal C*-completion is the same full matrix algebra.

For $n\ge0$, let $\mathcal P_n$ be the set of subsets of $\{1,\ldots,n\}$, and let $\mathcal F_n=\ell^2(\mathcal P_n)$ with orthonormal basis $e_S$ for $S\in\mathcal P_n$. For $1\le j\le n$ define operators on this finite-dimensional Hilbert space by

$$ c_j e_S=\begin{cases}0&j\notin S,\\(-1)^{|\{s\in S:s<j\}|}e_{S\setminus\{j\}}&j\in S,\end{cases}\qquad c_j^\dagger e_S=\begin{cases}(-1)^{|\{s\in S:s<j\}|}e_{S\cup\{j\}}&j\notin S,\\0&j\in S.\end{cases} $$

Then $c_j^\dagger$ is the Hilbert-space adjoint of $c_j$, and $a_j\mapsto c_j$, $a_j^\dagger\mapsto c_j^\dagger$ defines a $*$-representation $\pi_n:\mathsf{CAR}^{\mathrm{alg}}_n\to\operatorname{End}(\mathcal F_n)$. Put $N_j=c_j^\dagger c_j$ and $P_\varnothing=\prod_{j=1}^n(I-N_j)$, with the empty product equal to $I$. For $S=\{i_1<\cdots<i_p\}$ and $T=\{j_1<\cdots<j_q\}$, set

$$ E_{S,T}=c_{i_1}^\dagger\cdots c_{i_p}^\dagger P_\varnothing c_{j_q}\cdots c_{j_1}, $$

with empty operator products equal to $I$. Then $E_{S,T}e_U=\delta_{T,U}e_S$. Consequently the image of $\pi_n$ is all of $\operatorname{End}(\mathcal F_n)\cong M_{2^n}(\mathbb C)$.

A **real Hilbert space** is a real inner-product space $H$ ([[def-real-and-complex-inner-product-space]]) whose induced-length metric is complete in the sense of [[def-complete-metric-space]]: every Cauchy sequence in $H$ for the norm $\|v\|=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle}$ ([[cor-inner-product-induces-a-norm]]) converges to a point of $H$. A **complex Hilbert space** is a complex inner-product space with the same completeness property, so that a Hilbert space is exactly a real or complex inner-product space that is a Banach space for its induced norm ([[def-banach-space]]).

**The completion convention is the Cauchy-sequence one.**
[[def-banach-space]] defines completeness by convergence of Cauchy sequences, and this page keeps that convention throughout. It is weaker than $\sigma$-completeness — the assertion that every decreasing sequence of nonempty closed subsets with diameters tending to zero has a nonempty intersection. The two agree in ZFC, but Blackadar, Farah and Karagila note that the closest-point theorem on a $\sigma$-complete inner-product space is provable in ZF, whereas the Cauchy-complete form used below consumes the Axiom of Countable Choice; nothing here silently imports the stronger notion.

Let $\mathbb F$ be $\mathbb R$ or $\mathbb C$, with **conjugation** $z\mapsto\overline z$
the identity on $\mathbb R$ and complex conjugation on $\mathbb C$
([[def-complex-conjugate-real-imaginary-part-and-modulus]]). A **real** or
**complex inner-product space** is an $\mathbb F$-vector space $V$ together with
an inner product $\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle:V\times V\to\mathbb F$ in the sense
of [[def-inner-product-space]]: for all $u,v,w\in V$ and $a,b\in\mathbb F$,

$$\langle au+bv,w\rangle=a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle,\qquad \langle u,v\rangle=\overline{\langle v,u\rangle},\qquad \langle v,v\rangle\ge0,\quad \langle v,v\rangle=0\iff v=0 .$$

**Conjugate-linearity in the second argument.** Conjugate symmetry together with
linearity in the first argument gives, for all $w\in V$,

$$\langle w,au+bv\rangle=\overline{\langle au+bv,w\rangle}=\overline{a\langle u,w\rangle+b\langle v,w\rangle}=\overline a\,\langle w,u\rangle+\overline b\,\langle w,v\rangle .$$

**Induced length.** The **induced length**, or inner-product norm, of $v$ is

$$\|v\|:=\sqrt{\langle v,v\rangle},$$

which is exactly the published [[def-inner-product-norm]]: positive definiteness
makes $\langle v,v\rangle$ a nonnegative real with a unique nonnegative square
root, so that $\|v\|\ge0$, $\|v\|=0$ exactly for $v=0$, and
$\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2$.

**The convention on this page.** Every inner-product space below is real or
complex in this sense, the pairing is linear in the first argument and
conjugate-linear in the second, and $\|v\|$ always denotes the induced length.
In the real case conjugation is the identity and $|z|$ is the absolute value of
$\mathbb R$; in the complex case they are complex conjugation and the complex
modulus. All statements below are therefore written once and read in either
scalar field.

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field. Write

$$\mathcal B(X,Y) := \{T:X\to Y : T \text{ is a bounded linear operator}\}.$$

This is a subspace of the vector space $\mathcal L(X,Y)$ of
[[def-vector-space-of-linear-maps]], with the same pointwise operations:

$$(S+T)(x) := Sx+Tx,\qquad (\lambda T)(x) := \lambda\,Tx.$$

If $X=Y$, write

$$\mathcal B(X) := \mathcal B(X,X).$$

Let $X$ and $Y$ be normed spaces over the same scalar field, and let
$T:X\to Y$ be bounded in the sense of [[def-bounded-linear-operator]]. The
**operator norm** of $T$ is

$$\|T\| := \sup\{\|Tx\| : x \in X,\ \|x\| \le 1\}.$$

The set on the right contains $0$ and every bound $C$ for $T$ bounds it
above. Thus its finite real supremum exists by the proved least-upper-bound
property of the library's real field ([[cor-cauchy-reals-lub-complete]]).
In particular every number strictly below the supremum is exceeded by a
member of this set; otherwise it would be a smaller upper bound. No choice
principle is used for this assertion.

The same number is the least bound of $T$:

$$\|T\| = \inf\{C \ge 0 : \|Tx\| \le C\|x\| \text{ for all } x \in X\}.$$

If $X \ne \{0\}$, positive homogeneity also gives

$$\|T\| = \sup\{\|Tx\| : \|x\| = 1\}.$$

When $X = \{0\}$, the unit sphere is empty and the unit-ball supremum is $0$,
so $\|T\| = 0$.

Let $V,W$ be inner product spaces ([[def-inner-product-space]]) over the same field and let $T:V\to W$ be linear ([[def-linear-map]]). An **adjoint** of $T$ is a linear map $T^*:W\to V$ such that

$$\langle Tv,w\rangle_W=\langle v,T^*w\rangle_V$$

for every $v\in V$ and $w\in W$. Existence is not part of the definition; in finite dimensions it will follow from Riesz representation.

For all vectors $x,y$ in a real or complex inner-product space,

$$|\langle x,y\rangle|\le\|x\|\,\|y\| ,$$

with equality if and only if $x$ and $y$ are linearly dependent.

For every set $I$, the complex square-summable family space $\ell^2(I,\mathbb C)$ with its canonical norm and inner product from [[def-square-summable-family-on-an-arbitrary-index-set]] is complete. Thus it is a complex Hilbert space. Its finitely supported families are dense, and the coordinate vectors form an orthonormal basis. This result uses no choice principle.

derivations.claim: Restrict the given family to its first $n$ modes. The quotient universal property of [[def-finite-mode-car-algebra]] gives the finite algebraic $*$-homomorphism on generators, and [F2] identifies it with a contractive unital $*$-representation $\rho_n:\mathsf{CAR}_n\to\mathcal B(H)$. If $m\le n$, the maps $\rho_n\circ\iota_{m,n}$ and $\rho_m$ agree on all generators of $\mathsf{CAR}_m$, so uniqueness of the finite quotient map gives $\rho_n\circ\iota_{m,n}=\rho_m$.

Let $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{fin}}(\mathbb N)$ be all finite subsets of $\mathbb N$, and let $\mathcal F_\infty=\ell^2(\mathcal P_{\mathrm{fin}}(\mathbb N))$ with coordinate vectors $e_S$. By [F8], this is a complex Hilbert space, the vectors $e_S$ are an orthonormal basis, and their finite span is dense. Define $c_j e_S=0$ if $j\notin S$, and $c_j e_S=(-1)^{|\{s\in S:s<j\}|}e_{S\setminus\{j\}}$ if $j\in S$; define $c_j^\dagger$ by the reverse toggle with the same sign. Each map is a partial isometry on the basis and extends boundedly, and the coefficient of each reverse basis transition shows $c_j^\dagger$ is its adjoint. For any finite set of indices, choose $n$ containing them; under the decomposition of the basis into first-$n$ and tail subsets, the first $n$ operators act as the finite occupation representation tensored with the identity. Hence the CAR hold for every pair of indices. The finite universal property gives compatible contractive representations of all $\mathsf{CAR}_n$ on $\mathcal F_\infty$, which extend to a representation $\pi_\infty$ of the inductive limit.

Define $\rho_0$ on $\mathsf{CAR}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ by $\rho_0(x)=\rho_n(x)$ whenever $x\in\mathsf{CAR}_n$. Compatibility in step 1.1 makes this well defined, and contractivity at each stage gives $\|\rho_0(x)\|\le\|x\|$. The space $\mathcal B(H)$ is complete: for an operator-norm Cauchy sequence $(S_k)$, each $(S_kx)$ converges in $H$; its pointwise limit $Sx$ is linear and bounded because $(\|S_k\|)$ is bounded, and taking the pointwise limit in the uniform Cauchy bound shows $\|S_k-S\|\to0$. Thus $\rho_0$ extends uniquely and contractively to the completion. Products pass to limits by $\|AB\|\le\|A\|\|B\|$. For any bounded operator $A$ with a specified adjoint, [F6] and [F7] give $\|A^*y\|=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}|\langle A^*y,x\rangle|=\sup_{\|x\|\le1}|\langle Ax,y\rangle|\le\|A\|\|y\|$, hence $\|A^*\|\le\|A\|$. Conjugating [F6] shows $A$ is the adjoint of $A^*$; uniqueness gives $(A^*)^*=A$, so applying the same inequality to $A^*$ yields $\|A^*\|=\|A\|$. Therefore if $S_k\to S$, the adjoints $S_k^*$ are Cauchy and converge to some $R$; passing to the limit in [F6] gives $\langle Sx,y\rangle=\langle x,Ry\rangle$, so $R$ is the adjoint of $S$. Thus the extension preserves $*$ and is a unital $*$-homomorphism.

Under the basis bijection $\mathcal P_{\mathrm{fin}}(\mathbb N)\cong\mathcal P_n\times\mathcal P_{\mathrm{fin}}(\{n+1,n+2,\ldots\})$, the first $n$ toggle signs depend only on the first subset coordinate because every tail index is larger than every mode $j\le n$. Thus the restriction of $\pi_\infty$ to $\mathsf{CAR}_n$ is the finite matrix representation acting identically on each tail coordinate. The tail contains the empty subset, so it is nonzero; by the isometric amplification statement in [F2], $\|\pi_\infty(x)\|=\|x\|_{\mathsf{CAR}_n}$ for every $x\in\mathsf{CAR}_n$.

For any bounded CAR representation $\sigma$ and $x\in\mathsf{CAR}_n$, its restriction is contractive by [F2], so $\|\sigma(x)\|\le\|x\|_{\mathsf{CAR}_n}$. Step 2.2 supplies a representation attaining this norm. Therefore the supremum over all representations equals the inductive-limit norm on each finite stage. Every element of $\mathsf{CAR}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ lies in some finite stage, so the universal norm is finite and equals the inductive-limit norm on the entire union. Step 1.2 proves the representing family is nonempty. The extension in step 2.1 is unique because $\mathsf{CAR}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ is dense.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a braided fusion category and let $\mathcal M,\mathcal N$ be finite semisimple right $\mathcal C$-module categories. A **relative Deligne product** $\mathcal M\boxtimes_{\mathcal C}\mathcal N$ in $\operatorname{Mod}(\mathcal C)$ means a finite semisimple right $\mathcal C$-module category $\mathcal P$ equipped with an exact bilinear functor $b:\mathcal M\times\mathcal N\to\mathcal P$ that is balanced over the middle $\mathcal C$-action and compatible with the outer right $\mathcal C$-action, and is universal among such functors: for every finite semisimple right $\mathcal C$-module category $\mathcal D$, composition with $b$ gives an equivalence between right $\mathcal C$-module functors $\mathcal P\to\mathcal D$ and exact bilinear middle-balanced right $\mathcal C$-module functors $\mathcal M\times\mathcal N\to\mathcal D$.

For the balancing convention, a right module category $\mathcal N$ is regarded as a left module category by $X\triangleright n:=n\odot X$. Its left module associator $(X\otimes Y)\triangleright n\to X\triangleright(Y\triangleright n)$ is the composite of $n\odot c_{Y,X}^{-1}$ with the inverse right-module associator. “Balanced” means that $b(m\odot X,n)\cong b(m,X\triangleright n)$ naturally in all variables, compatibly with the unit and associativity constraints. This definition fixes the universal property and the braiding convention; it does not assert that a product exists.

Let $\mathcal C$ be a braided fusion category and let $A,B$ be separable algebra objects, with bimodule sections $\sigma_A,\sigma_B$. Give $A\otimes B$ the braided tensor-product algebra structure from [[thm-braided-category-tensor-product-algebra-structure]]. A separability section is
$$\sigma_{A\otimes B}=(1_A\otimes c_{B,A}^{-1}\otimes1_B)\circ(\sigma_A\otimes\sigma_B):A\otimes B\longrightarrow(A\otimes B)\otimes(A\otimes B).$$
This is an $A\otimes B$-bimodule map and its composite with multiplication is the identity.

Let $A,B$ be separable algebra objects in a fusion category $\mathcal C$. The categories of left $A$-modules, right $B$-modules and $A$-$B$ bimodules are finite semisimple. This assertion is valid in any characteristic in which the stated separability sections exist. In particular the left $A$-modules, with action $P\odot X=P\otimes X$, form a finite semisimple right $\mathcal C$-module category.

In a monoidal category $\mathcal C$, an **algebra object** is an object $A$ with multiplication $m_A:A\otimes A\to A$ and unit $\eta_A:\mathbf1\to A$ satisfying associativity and unit equations with the associator and unitors of $\mathcal C$. It is **separable** if there is an $A$-bimodule morphism $\sigma_A:A\to A\otimes A$ with $m_A\sigma_A=1_A$. The composite $e_A=\sigma_A\eta_A:\mathbf1\to A\otimes A$ is its **separability element**. It satisfies $m_Ae_A=\eta_A$ and the centrality equation
$$ (m_A\otimes1_A)\circ(1_A\otimes e_A)=(1_A\otimes m_A)\circ(e_A\otimes1_A):A\longrightarrow A\otimes A,$$
with associators inserted. In element notation these are $\sum_i x_i y_i=1_A$ and $\sum_i a x_i\otimes y_i=\sum_i x_i\otimes y_i a$.

A **left $A$-module** is an object $M\in\mathcal C$ with an associative unital action $l_M:A\otimes M\to M$; a **right $A$-module** has an associative unital action $r_M:M\otimes A\to M$. Write $\operatorname{Mod}^{l}_{\mathcal C}(A)$ and $\operatorname{Mod}^{r}_{\mathcal C}(A)$ for their categories and module morphisms. The category of left $A$-modules is a right $\mathcal C$-module category by $M\odot X:=M\otimes X$, with left $A$-action obtained by associating $A\otimes(M\otimes X)$ to $(A\otimes M)\otimes X$ and applying $l_M\otimes1_X$, and the inherited associator and unitor. An **$A$-$B$ bimodule** is an object $X\in\mathcal C$ with commuting left and right actions $A\otimes X\to X$ and $X\otimes B\to X$, each associative and unital. A bimodule morphism preserves both actions.

The **regular $A$-$A$ bimodule** is the object $A$ with both actions given by $m_A$.

Given an $A$-$B$ bimodule $X$ and a $B$-$D$ bimodule $Y$, a morphism $q:X\otimes Y\to Z$ is **balanced over $B$** if
$$q\circ(r_X\otimes1_Y)=q\circ(1_X\otimes l_Y):X\otimes B\otimes Y\longrightarrow Z.$$
A relative tensor product $X\otimes_B Y$, when it exists, is an object with a balanced map $q_B:X\otimes Y\to X\otimes_B Y$ universal among balanced maps. Existence is not part of this definition.

derivations.claim: The left-module presentation reverses the algebra-bimodule $1$-morphism orientation: a module functor $\operatorname{Mod}^l(A)\to\operatorname{Mod}^l(B)$ is represented by a $B$-$A$ bimodule, while the algebra convention $A\to B$ uses $A$-$B$ bimodules. Thus the algebra presentation of this module $2$-category uses the $1$-morphism opposite of that algebra bicategory. Tensor multiplication on objects is unchanged. Under this passage the evaluation and coevaluation arrows exchange, and left and right dual roles exchange; both dual orientations have been constructed separately. Preserve the positive braided tensor algebra K=A⊗B. Let P=Mod^l_C(K). Define b(M,N)=M⊗N, with K-action `(l_M⊗l_N)(1_A⊗c_{B,M}⊗1_N)`.

Naturality and the hexagons prove its action equation exactly as for the positive tensor-algebra multiplication. Define balance by `1_M⊗c_{N,X}^{-1}: MXN→MNX`; this is K-linear: expand c_{B,MX}, cancel the c_{B,X} against c_{N,X}^{-1} by naturality with l_N, and the remaining composite is the target K-action. The balance/unit equation is the braiding unit equation. For balance associativity on $MXYN$, both composites are the inverse braid taking $XYN$ to $NYX$: move $Y$ behind $N$ and then $X$ behind $NY$, or move $XY$ behind $N$ and then interchange $X,Y$ by $c_{Y,X}^{-1}$. The inverse hexagon expands both to the same three inverse crossings. Compatibility with the outer right action is the other inverse hexagon. Hence b is a balanced right-module functor. It is exact and bilinear because all tensor functors in a fusion category are exact.

Here is a proof of universality which also specifies its action on transformations. A right K-object d in a finite semisimple right C-module category D is an object equipped with r:d⊙K→d satisfying the algebra action equations. It determines a module functor H_d:P→D by `H_d(L)=d⊙_K L`,

constructed as the image of the separability idempotent `(r⊙l_L)(1_d⊙e_K⊙1_L)` on d⊙L. Its image exists because D is finite semisimple. The usual centrality and unit equations for e_K show this image corepresents K-balanced maps, just as for the ordinary bimodule supplier: the idempotent is fixed by every balanced map; conversely its projection is balanced. No new coequalizer existence theorem is being assumed. This construction is functorial in L and K-linear maps d→d'.

Conversely any module functor H:P→D is canonically H_d with d=H(K). Its right action is H(m_K):H(K⊗K)≅H(K)⊙K→H(K). On free modules K⊗X, its module constraint gives H(K⊗X)≅d⊙X. Every K-module L is a retract of K⊗L: the action is the retraction and the section is `(1_K⊗l_L)(e_K⊗1_L)`. This section is K-linear by centrality, and its action composite is 1_L. Hence the free-module comparison extends uniquely to all retracts. To check naturality it suffices to check free maps. Such a map K⊗X→K⊗Y is uniquely `(m_K⊗1_Y)(1_K⊗f)` for f:X→K⊗Y obtained by inserting η_K; H and H_d agree on this expression by the definition of r. Transformations agree precisely when their value at K is K-linear. This proves an equivalence of categories, including transformations, between module functors P→D and right K-objects in D. For a balanced module functor F:Mod^l(A)×Mod^l(B)→D, put d=F(A,B). Denote its outer constraint by `δ:F(M,NX)→F(M,N)⊙X` and its balance by β. Put `θ=δβ:F(MX,N)→F(M,N)⊙X`. Define `r_A=F(m_A,1_B) θ_{A,A,B}^{-1}:d⊙A→d`, `r_B=F(1_A,m_B) δ_{A,B,B}^{-1}:d⊙B→d`.

Naturality with the algebra multiplications proves their associative/unital action equations. Expanding the balance/outer compatibility square gives the precise exchange equation `r_A(r_B⊙1_A)=r_B(r_A⊙1_B)(1_d⊙c_{B,A}):d⊙B⊙A→d`.

For an explicit verification, replace θ by δβ, move each multiplication through δ by its naturality, and through β by naturality in its module arguments. The residual two routes move the free B slot past the free A slot. The balance-associativity equation for the chosen inverse left conversion replaces that move by c_{B,A}; its inverse crossing is cancelled by the inverse in θ^-1. The remaining maps are F(m_A,m_B) on both routes. Thus `r=r_B(r_A⊙1_B)` is a right K-action: its iterated action on dABAB first moves the middle B past A by c_{B,A}, then uses the two individual action equations, exactly giving r(1_d⊙m_K). This proves the action equation without assuming ordinary commuting actions.

The functor H_d b is canonically equivalent to F. On free pairs first use δ to identify $F(AX,BY)$ with $F(AX,B)\odot Y$, and then θ on the first factor, to obtain `F(A⊗X,B⊗Y)≅d⊙X⊙Y`. Meanwhile the positive crossing `1_A⊗c_{B,X}⊗1_Y` is a K-linear isomorphism `K⊗X⊗Y→b(A⊗X,B⊗Y)`;

it identifies H_d b on this pair with d⊙X⊙Y. The two identifications commute with arbitrary free A-module and B-module morphisms: express such morphisms by their adjoint maps X→A⊗X' and Y→B⊗Y', then use r_A,r_B respectively. For a simultaneous morphism the exchange equation is exactly the required compatibility of the two orders. Every M,N is a retract of its free module by the displayed separability section, so this natural equivalence extends to all pairs by taking images of the two commuting retract idempotents. The construction respects the balance and outer action because it does so on free pairs, where these equations are the already verified β,δ equations. Thus composition with b is essentially surjective on balanced functors.

A transformation between two balanced functors is determined on free pairs by its component at (A,B), using θ,δ, and then on all pairs by retracts. Naturality with m_A and m_B says exactly that this component preserves r_A,r_B, equivalently the K-action r. Conversely any K-linear component gives such a transformation via H_d. Consequently composition with b is fully faithful and is the required equivalence of categories. This proves the exact stated universal property, not merely existence of a bilinear functor.

Finite semisimplicity of P follows from separability of K: module Hom spaces are images of the averaging idempotent on Hom_C(M,N), so are finite dimensional; every module is a retract of a free module, and the finitely many free modules K⊗S_i for simple S_i of C form a finite additive generator. Its endomorphism algebra is semisimple because any module subobject splits by averaging an underlying splitting. Therefore the module category is finite semisimple. It is a right C-module category by the inherited tensor action. The preceding argument applies to arbitrary D, so uniqueness of representing objects makes the answer independent of the chosen algebra presentations, with a canonical equivalence preserving b.

For module functors G:M→M',H:N→N', apply the universal property to b'(G×H); its balanced structure is inherited from the module constraints of G,H. This defines G⊠H. For module-natural transformations use full faithfulness to define their product. Identity and composite comparison maps are the unique maps whose pullbacks to b equal the identity or the corresponding composite constraint. Their associativity, unit and interchange equations hold by full faithfulness, since after pullback they are the same equation for ordinary functor composition.

Both parenthesizations of three module categories represent the category of three-variable exact functors balanced in the two adjacent slots, with outer right-module compatibility. This follows by applying the just-proved equivalence twice; the same free/retract argument shows that no balanced transformations are lost. Their comparison is therefore the unique equivalence preserving the universal three-variable functor, with its specified natural isomorphism. For the regular module category C, the action functor M×C→M (and the converted left action C×M→M) has the universal property by inserting the unit object and applying balance. These give the unitors. On four variables the two pentagon composites have the same pullback comparison to the universal four-variable functor. Full faithfulness gives the unique pentagonator modification; on five variables the two composites of these modifications have identical pullback, hence are equal. The unitor triangle modification and all its compatibility equations follow in exactly the same way from the three-variable functor with a unit slot. This is the weak monoidal 2-category coherence assertion: one should say 'canonical modifications' rather than incorrectly demanding literal equality of unchosen equivalences. Naturality with G,H and their transformations follows by pulling back to the same multivariable functor. Thus the product supplies all morphism levels and weak coherence required in the carrier statement.

risk_review.notes: Read all thirteen steps and all seven suppliers, including the full reconstruction-to-separable-algebras proof. The statement assumes separable presentations, so the construction itself does not impose a hidden characteristic-zero condition. The negative left-action conversion and balance MXN→MNX use c_{N,X}^{−1}; this fixes the positive c_{B,A} multiplication on K=A⊗B. The balance/outer equations give r_A(r_B⊙1)=r_B(r_A⊙1)(1⊙c_{B,A}), exactly the right K-action equation. Free modules and their explicit separability retracts identify module functors out of Mod^l(K) with right K-objects in arbitrary target D. Free-pair comparison plus the exchange equation proves essential surjectivity, while evaluation at (A,B) and retracts proves full faithfulness on transformations. Finite semisimplicity, zero cases, and independence of presentation follow with the same universal property. Iterated universal functors give the associators and unitors and unique comparison modifications; full faithfulness proves pentagon/triangle coherence without asserting literal equality of arbitrary choices. Checked Décoppet §1, pp.2–3, and Douglas–Reutter Construction 2.1.19; the local proof establishes the general braided claim.
